title: X API Expansions Start Billing on 22 Nov 2026: What It Does to Social Listening and Reply-Tool Costs (Worked Math, Python Estimator, Ways to Cut It)
author: appierun
summary: If your code calls the X API with expansions=author_id , your bill is about to change. On the pay-per-use (PPU) plan, the user, post, media, poll and place objects that come back in the includes section of a response have not counted toward usage. From 22 November 2026 they do, at the same rate as a direct lookup. For a keyword monitor that pulls each post's author, that can mean the author objects cost more than the posts themselves. This post covers what X announced, which rates X's own pages show today, three worked cost examples with labeled inputs, a standard-library Python script that estimates the change from responses you've saved, and ways to cut the bill. Rates and rules below come from three X pages opened on 16 Nov 2026: the X Developer Community announcement [Inform] X API PPU - Expansions Update (posted 23 Oct 2026), the docs page X API pay-per-usage pricing and credits , and the docs page Usage and Billing . All prices are in USD and are as of 16 Nov 2026. X says prices are subject to change and that current rates are always in the Developer Console, so check there before you budget. Appie details are from appie.run/pricing and appie.run/twitter-marketing, checked 16 Nov 2026. The estimator script was tested on Python 3.13.5 against fixture JSON files, not live API calls. Disclosure: Appie.run publishes this article. Appie's Twitter Marketing app, covered in one short section near the end, is our product. Nothing else in this post depends on it. What X announced The forum post from the X Developer Platform team says that on PPU, "usage is based on the data objects the API returns," and that "right now, objects that come back through expansions aren't counted towards usage." Then the change: "From November 22nd, objects returned through expansions will be billed at the standard PPU rate for that resource, the same as direct lookups. This covers post, user, media, poll and place expansions." The post lists the rates: Object returned through an expansion: Post; Rate per resource (X forum post, read 16 Nov 2026): $0.005; Also on the docs pricing page today?: Yes, as "Posts: Read" $0.005 per resource Object returned through an expansion: User; Rate per resource (X forum post, read 16 Nov 2026): $0.010; Also on the docs pricing page today?: Yes, as "User: Read" $0.010 per resource Object returned through an expansion: Media; Rate per resource (X forum post, read 16 Nov 2026): $0.005; Also on the docs pricing page today?: No, not listed Object returned through an expansion: Poll; Rate per resource (X forum post, read 16 Nov 2026): $0.005; Also on the docs pricing page today?: No, not listed Object returned through an expansion: Place; Rate per resource (X forum post, read 16 Nov 2026): $0.005; Also on the docs pricing page today?: No, not listed X calls this "not a new pricing model," and that is accurate: the Post and User rates are the same ones you already pay for data . What changes is how many objects count. Some gaps you should know about, because X's pages don't fill them as of 16 Nov 2026: No time of day or time zone. The post says "November 22nd." X's pricing docs say deduplication resets at midnight UTC, so the safe plan is to treat 00:00 UTC on 22 Nov as the start. That is 7:00 PM EST and 4:00 PM PST on Saturday 21 Nov, and 5:30 AM IST on 22 Nov. This is our planning assumption, not X's statement. The docs haven't caught up. The Expansions page doesn't mention billing, the pricing page has no Media, Poll or Place rows, and the changelog had no entry about this change when we checked. Owned Reads. Your own app reading your own mentions ( GET /2/users/{id}/mentions ) is billed at $0.001 per resource as an Owned Read. X doesn't say whether the users expanded on that call get the $0.001 rate or the standard $0.010. The post says "standard PPU rate for that resource," so the examples below use $0.010. The 3 million cap. PPU is capped at 3 million Post reads per monthly billing cycle. X doesn't say whether expanded posts count toward that cap. The billing rules that shape the math These come from the two docs pages and apply to every example below: Reads are charged per resource returned. Ten posts in data are ten Post reads. With the change, three distinct users in includes.users are three User reads on top. Daily deduplication. "All resources are deduplicated within a 24-hour UTC day window," and this "applies to all billable resources (Posts, users, etc.)". The same author on 40 posts in one UTC day is charged once that day and again the next day. X calls deduplication "a soft guarantee" and says edge cases such as outages may not be deduplicated. Failed requests aren't billed. "Only successful responses that return data are billed." Spending limits and auto-recharge are set in the Developer Console. When a spending limit is reached, requests are blocked until the next billing cycle. Worked math: three common workloads Every volume below is an example input , chosen to show how the change scales. None of them is a measured average. Replace them with your own counts (the script in the next section gets them from your saved responses). Example 1: keyword listening with recent search A monitor runs GET /2/tweets/search/recent for a brand name and a few competitor phrases, with expansions=author_id,referenced_tweets.id,attachments.media_keys . Example inputs per month: 1,000 matching posts; 700 author objects after daily dedup (some authors post more than once a day); 250 referenced posts (the post being replied to, quoted or reposted); 200 media objects. Line: Posts in data : 1,000 × $0.005; Before 22 Nov: $5.00; From 22 Nov: $5.00 Line: Authors in includes.users : 700 × $0.010; Before 22 Nov: $0.00; From 22 Nov: $7.00 Line: Referenced posts in includes.tweets : 250 × $0.005; Before 22 Nov: $0.00; From 22 Nov: $1.25 Line: Media in includes.media : 200 × $0.005; Before 22 Nov: $0.00; From 22 Nov: $1.00 Line: Total ; Before 22 Nov: $5.00 ; From 22 Nov: $14.25 The same query costs 2.85 times as much, and the authors alone cost more than the posts. At 10 times the volume (10,000 posts, 7,000 authors, 2,500 referenced posts, 2,000 media) the total goes from $50.00 to $142.50. Example 2: a reply tool that fetches thread context A reply tool may pull the whole conversation before a reply is written, so the reply makes sense: a search on conversation_id:<id> with expansions=author_id,in_reply_to_user_id . Example inputs per month: 300 threads opened for triage; 12 posts per thread on average; 8 distinct users per thread. Line: Thread posts: 300 × 12 = 3,600 × $0.005; Before 22 Nov: $18.00; From 22 Nov: $18.00 Line: Thread users: 300 × 8 = 2,400 × $0.010; Before 22 Nov: $0.00; From 22 Nov: $24.00 Line: Total ; Before 22 Nov: $18.00 ; From 22 Nov: $42.00 If your tool also sends replies through the API, writes are a separate line: X lists "Post: Create" at $0.015 per request and "Post: Create (with URL)" at $0.200 per request. A reply with a link costs about 13 times a reply without one. Example 3: your own mentions on the Owned Reads rate An app reads mentions of its own account through GET /2/users/{id}/mentions with expansions=author_id . Example inputs per month: 2,000 mentions; 1,200 author objects after daily dedup. Line: Mentions as Owned Reads: 2,000 × $0.001; Before 22 Nov: $2.00; From 22 Nov (assuming the standard User rate): $2.00 Line: Authors: 1,200 × $0.010; Before 22 Nov: $0.00; From 22 Nov (assuming the standard User rate): $12.00 Line: Total ; Before 22 Nov: $2.00 ; From 22 Nov (assuming the standard User rate): $14.00 This is the workload where the change hurts most in relative terms, because the posts are on a 1,000-for-$1 rate and the users aren't. If X applies the Owned Reads rate to these users, the new line is $1.20 instead of $12.00. Check your Developer Console in the first days after 22 Nov to see which rate you are charged. Estimate your own change with Python (standard library only) Guessing volumes is the weak part of the examples above. If you log raw API responses, you can count the objects directly. Save each response as JSON in a folder per UTC day (for example responses/2026-11-23/page1.json ) and run this: #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Estimate X API pay-per-use cost for saved v2 responses, before and after expansion objects are billed. Rates: X Developer Community post "[Inform] X API PPU - Expansions Update" and docs.x.com pricing, read 16 Nov 2026. Edit RATES if your Developer Console shows different numbers.""" import json import sys from pathlib import Path RATES = { # USD per resource "posts" : 0.005 , # data[] posts and includes.tweets "users" : 0.010 , "media" : 0.005 , "polls" : 0.005 , "places" : 0.005 , } INCLUDE_KEYS = { "tweets" : "posts" , "users" : "users" , "media" : "media" , "polls" : "polls" , "places" : "places" } def object_ids ( resp ) : """Yield (kind, id, from_expansion) for every billable object in a response.""" data = resp . get ( "data" ) or [ ] if isinstance ( data , dict ) : data = [ data ] for post in data : yield "posts" , post [ "id" ] , False for key , kind in INCLUDE_KEYS . items ( ) : for obj in resp . get ( "includes" , { } ) . get ( key , [ ] ) : oid = obj . get ( "id" ) or obj . get ( "media_key" ) yield kind , oid , True def main ( paths ) : # One set per UTC day folder mimics X's daily dedup. direct , expanded = { } , { } for p in paths : day = Path ( p ) . parent . name # e.g. responses/2026-11-23/page1.json resp = json . loads ( Path ( p ) . read_text ( ) ) for kind , oid , from_exp in object_ids ( resp ) : seen_direct = direct . setdefault ( kind , set ( ) ) seen_exp = expanded . setdefault ( kind , set ( ) ) key = ( day , oid ) if from_exp : if key not in seen_direct : seen_exp . add ( key ) else : seen_direct . add ( key ) seen_exp . discard ( key ) before = sum ( len ( direct . get ( k , ( ) ) ) * r for k , r in RATES . items ( ) ) extra = sum ( len ( expanded . get ( k , ( ) ) ) * r for k , r in RATES . items ( ) ) print ( f "{'object':<8}{'direct':>8}{'expanded':>10}{'new cost':>10}" ) for k , r in RATES . items ( ) : d , e = len ( direct . get ( k , ( ) ) ) , len ( expanded . get ( k , ( ) ) ) print ( f "{k:<8}{d:>8}{e:>10}{e * r:>10.3f}" ) print ( f "before 22 Nov: ${before:.3f}" ) print ( f "from 22 Nov: ${before + extra:.3f} (+${extra:.3f})" ) if __name__ == "__main__" : main ( sys . argv [ 1 : ] ) Run it with python3 x_expansion_cost.py responses/*/*.json . Here is real output from a fixture of four saved search pages over two UTC days (50 posts per page, 40 possible authors, some replies and photos): object direct expanded new cost posts 200 52 0.260 users 0 74 0.740 media 0 40 0.200 polls 0 0 0.000 places 0 0 0.000 before 22 Nov: $1.000 from 22 Nov: $2.200 (+$1.200) The 200 posts cost $1.00 either way; the new $1.20 is all includes . The 74 user objects are counted per UTC day, so an author who posts on both days is charged twice and an author who posts ten times in one day is charged once. Limits: the script applies standard rates everywhere, so it overstates the Owned Reads case in Example 3, and it can't model the edge cases X's "soft guarantee" on dedup leaves open. Treat the total as an estimate and compare it with the Developer Console after 22 Nov. Ways to cut the bill Roughly in the order we'd do them. Audit every expansions= parameter. Search your codebase for expansions . Expansions are often copied from a docs example (X's own "Full post context" pattern asks for author_id,attachments.media_keys,referenced_tweets.id ) and never trimmed. If your listening dashboard never renders images, attachments.media_keys is pure cost from 22 Nov. In Example 1 that is $1.00 of $14.25. Cache users across days instead of expanding on every call. Deduplication resets every midnight UTC, so a regular author is charged again every day you expand them. Drop the author_id expansion from the search, keep tweet.fields=author_id so each post still carries its author's ID, and call GET /2/users?ids= (up to 100 IDs per request, same $0.010 User rate) only for IDs not already in your cache. Example input: if Example 1's 700 daily author objects are 350 distinct accounts over the month, a 30-day cache cuts that line from $7.00 to $3.50. Filter before you enrich. Score posts on their text first, then fetch context only for the ones a person will look at. If only 50 of Example 1's 250 replies are worth answering, fetching their parent posts with GET /2/tweets?ids= costs $0.25 instead of $1.25. Run the second pass in the same UTC day as the search so any post you fetch again is deduplicated. Tighten the query. -is:retweet , lang: and excluding your own handle (operators listed in X's search operators docs) cut posts and every object those posts pull into includes . A repost is the worst case: you pay for the repost, the original in includes.tweets , and possibly the original's author. Stay inside one UTC day. If you poll several times a day, schedule the runs so they don't straddle 00:00 UTC. In November that is midnight in London, 1 AM in Berlin and 7 PM Eastern the evening before. Use Owned Reads where they apply. For your own account's mentions, the mentions timeline at $0.001 per post is far cheaper than searching for @yourhandle at $0.005, even if the expanded users end up at $0.010. Set a spending limit and watch usage. A spending limit in the Developer Console blocks requests when it's reached, which is better than finding a drained balance. X's docs also describe a Usage endpoint, GET /2/usage/tweets , that returns daily Post consumption, so you can compare the week before 22 Nov with the week after. Where Appie fits Appie is our product. Its Twitter Marketing app tracks your handle, keywords, competitors and buyer pain phrases in a Growth project. You start each scan yourself, X is scanned at most once a day, and you can generate a reply draft for any relevant post from that scan. Appie never posts: you copy the draft and post it from your own X account. It is not a real-time alerting tool. Per appie.run/pricing as of 16 Nov 2026, a Mention Scan costs 10 credits per Reddit or Twitter scan and a Response Draft costs 2 credits. The page says one dollar equals 100 credits. Example: one scan a day for 30 days is 300 credits; drafting 20 replies adds 40 credits, for 340. The Free plan has 500 credits once on signup and needs no credit card; Starter is $19/month for 2,000 credits and Standard is $49/month for 5,000. Limits, so you can compare fairly: Appie's pages don't say how many posts a scan covers, so there's no per-post cost to set against the examples above. Appie doesn't give you raw X API access or per-object control over what is fetched. And these are Appie's prices as listed today; we're not claiming they can't change, or that changes on X's side never affect us. If you keep your own script and only want help with the reply, Appie's free AI Reply Generator takes the post you're answering (pick "X (Twitter) Reply" as the source) and returns a draft you edit before sending. For the no-API route with saved searches, see How to monitor X (Twitter) mentions and reply without living in the app . FAQ What are X API expansions? A request parameter that pulls related objects (the post's author, the post it replies to or quotes, attached media, polls and places) into the includes section of the same response, so you don't need a second request. X's Expansions page lists them per object type. When does X start charging for expansions? 22 November 2026, per X's developer forum post of 23 Oct 2026. The post gives a date but no time or time zone. Because X's billing day runs on UTC, plan for 00:00 UTC on 22 Nov. How much does an expanded object cost? Per X's post, read 16 Nov 2026: $0.005 per post, $0.010 per user, $0.005 per media object, $0.005 per poll and $0.005 per place. The Post and User rates match X's docs pricing page. Media, Poll and Place weren't on the docs pricing page when we checked, so the forum post is the only X source for those three. Does deduplication apply to expanded objects? X's pricing page says deduplication within a 24-hour UTC day "applies to all billable resources (Posts, users, etc.)". The forum post doesn't address expansions and dedup specifically, so confirm in your Developer Console. Do user.fields or tweet.fields cost extra? X's post describes billing per data object returned, and fields add data to an object rather than adding objects. But X doesn't state this outright for fields, so test with a small request and check usage. Wrap-up The expansion change doesn't touch X's rates. It changes which objects count, and in all three examples above the biggest new line is users at $0.010 each. Before 22 Nov, grep for expansions , remove what you don't render, move author lookups behind a cache, and set a spending limit. Then run the estimator on a day of saved responses and compare it with the Developer Console in the first week after the change. RG, Founder, Appie.run

title: Audit Image Weight Across Your Sitemap with Python (Standard Library Only): Oversized Images, Missing Width/Height, Lazy Loading, CSV Report
author: appierun
summary: Image weight creeps up quietly. Someone uploads a 3000 pixel PNG straight from a design tool and the CMS shows it at 600 pixels wide. A theme update adds loading="lazy" to every image, including the hero at the top of the page. A gallery block drops the width and height attributes, so the text jumps down as each photo arrives. None of this breaks a page. It just makes it slower and jumpier, one upload at a time. This post builds an image weight auditor in Python using only the standard library ( urllib , urllib.robotparser , html.parser , xml.etree , struct , csv , concurrent.futures ). It reads your sitemap or sitemap index, fetches every page, collects each , and checks every unique image once. It gets the file size from a HEAD request's Content-Length and falls back to downloading the file when the server refuses HEAD or sends no length. It reads the real pixel size from the first bytes of PNG, GIF, JPEG and WebP files, compares that with the declared width , flags images with no width / height , and checks how loading="lazy" is used. Output is a CSV with one row per image per page, a console summary with the heaviest pages, and an exit code you can use in CI. web.dev's Browser-level image lazy loading for the web and Optimize Cumulative Layout Shift (showing "Last updated: Feb 7, 2025"), Chrome for Developers' Properly size images Lighthouse page, and Google Search Central's image SEO best practices (showing "Last updated 2026-03-02 UTC") were opened on 17 Nov 2026, and every statement attributed to them below comes from those pages. Appie free-tool descriptions are as of 17 Nov 2026, checked on the tool pages that day. The script was tested on Python 3.13.5 against a local fixture site with planted problems; the output below is real, from runs on 17 Nov 2026. Disclosure: Appie.run publishes this article. Two free tools mentioned near the end are ours. The script does not depend on them. Where this fits This is another script in a small standard-library series. An earlier one found images missing alt text across a sitemap , which is about what an image means. This one is about what an image costs: bytes, pixels, layout space and loading order. The most recent post measured click depth for every sitemap page . Same approach throughout: parse what the server returns, report what is there, and leave the judgment to a person. What the guidance actually says (and what it does not) Size. Google's image SEO page says "images are often the largest contributor to overall page size, which can make pages slow and expensive to load," and asks you to "apply the latest image optimization and responsive image techniques." The web.dev lazy loading article cites the HTTP Archive: images "usually take up more bandwidth than any other resource," and "At the 90th percentile, sites send over 5 MB of images on desktop and mobile." Pixels versus display size. Lighthouse's Properly size images page explains how it decides an image is too big: it "compares the size of the rendered image against the size of the actual image," accounting for device pixel ratio, and fails the image "If the rendered size is at least 4KiB smaller than the actual size." The page now carries a warning that this audit "has moved into the Improve image delivery insight as of Lighthouse 13." The principle is unchanged: "your page should never serve images that are larger than the version that's rendered on the user's screen." Width and height. The Optimize CLS article lists "Images without dimensions" first among "The most common causes of a poor CLS," and says: "Always include width and height size attributes on your images and video elements. Alternatively, reserve the required space with CSS aspect-ratio or similar." Modern browsers use those attributes to set a default aspect ratio before the image loads, so width: 100%; height: auto in CSS still works with them. Lazy loading. The lazy loading article describes loading="lazy" as deferring an image "until it reaches a calculated distance from the viewport," and gives a clear caution: "Don't lazy-load images that are likely to be in-viewport when the page loads, especially LCP images." It also notes that without width and height an image defaults to 0x0 pixels, so in a gallery "the browser might decide that all of them fit inside the viewport at the start" and load everything. What none of these pages give is a kilobyte limit for a single image. The script's default of 200 KB is my own starting line, not a Google or Lighthouse number. Change it with --max-kb and keep it the same between runs. The pixel check uses 2x the declared width by default ( --max-scale ) so that images exported for high density screens are not flagged. And the script cannot know where the fold is. It does not render the page, so it treats the first two images in the HTML as "probably above the fold" ( --eager-first , default 2, because a header logo is usually image one and the hero is image two). How the audit works Sitemap URLs. It reads a urlset or a sitemap index (recursively, gzip supported) and keeps every . robots.txt is respected for page fetches. Images per page. It parses each page's HTML and collects every in document order. Markup inside

title: Kiểm tra dữ liệu chứng chỉ trong file CSV bằng Python: ngày hợp lệ và trạng thái hiệu lực
author: nghiepvuvietnam
summary: Khi quản lý một danh sách giấy chứng nhận hay chứng chỉ trong file CSV, lỗi hay gặp nhất không nằm ở logic phức tạp mà ở dữ liệu: ô ngày để trống, ngày không tồn tại, ngày hết hạn đứng trước ngày cấp. Bài này viết một đoạn Python nhỏ, chỉ dùng thư viện chuẩn, để đọc CSV, kiểm tra từng dòng và phân loại trạng thái hiệu lực. Mã đã chạy thử trên Python 3.12. Bài toán Mỗi dòng gồm họ tên, tên chứng chỉ, ngày cấp và ngày hết hạn (có thể để trống nếu chứng chỉ không ghi thời hạn). Ta muốn: Đọc được dòng hợp lệ thành đối tượng có kiểu rõ ràng. Gom riêng các dòng lỗi kèm số dòng để người nhập sửa lại. Phân loại: không thời hạn, còn hạn, sắp hết hạn, đã hết hạn. Mã nguồn import csv , io from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import date , datetime DATA = """ho_ten,ten_chung_chi,ngay_cap,ngay_het_han An,Chung chi A,2023-03-10,2026-03-10 Binh,Chung chi B,2024-05-01, Chi,Chung chi A,2022-12-31,2025-12-31 Dung,Chung chi C,2025-02-30,2028-02-28 Hoa,Chung chi B,2026-01-15,2025-01-15 """ @dataclass class HoSo : ho_ten : str chung_chi : str ngay_cap : date ngay_het_han : date | None def doc_ngay ( s ) : s = s . strip ( ) return datetime . strptime ( s , "%Y-%m-%d" ) . date ( ) if s else None def doc_ho_so ( text ) : hop_le , loi = [ ] , [ ] for dong , r in enumerate ( csv . DictReader ( io . StringIO ( text ) ) , start = 2 ) : try : cap = doc_ngay ( r [ "ngay_cap" ] ) het = doc_ngay ( r [ "ngay_het_han" ] ) if het and het < cap : raise ValueError ( "ngay het han truoc ngay cap" ) hop_le . append ( HoSo ( r [ "ho_ten" ] , r [ "ten_chung_chi" ] , cap , het ) ) except ValueError as e : loi . append ( ( dong , r [ "ho_ten" ] , str ( e ) ) ) return hop_le , loi def trang_thai ( h , hom_nay , sap_het = 90 ) : if h . ngay_het_han is None : return "khong thoi han" con = ( h . ngay_het_han - hom_nay ) . days if con < 0 : return "da het han" return "sap het han" if con <= sap_het else "con han" if __name__ == "__main__" : hom_nay = date ( 2026 , 11 , 18 ) ds , loi = doc_ho_so ( DATA ) for h in ds : print ( h . ho_ten , "-" , trang_thai ( h , hom_nay ) ) for dong , ten , msg in loi : print ( "LOI dong" , dong , ten , ":" , msg ) Giải thích dataclass. HoSo giữ dữ liệu một dòng. Ngày hết hạn có kiểu date | None để thể hiện chứng chỉ không ghi thời hạn, thay vì dùng chuỗi rỗng. Bắt lỗi theo từng dòng. datetime.strptime tự từ chối ngày không tồn tại như 30/02, nên ta không cần viết thêm luật kiểm tra lịch. Lỗi được ghi vào danh sách loi kèm số dòng (bắt đầu từ 2 vì dòng 1 là tiêu đề), chương trình vẫn chạy tiếp các dòng còn lại. Luật nghiệp vụ. Điều kiện het < cap bắt trường hợp ngày hết hạn đứng trước ngày cấp, thường do nhập nhầm. Truyền ngày hiện tại vào hàm. trang_thai nhận hom_nay làm tham số thay vì gọi date.today() bên trong. Nhờ vậy kết quả lặp lại được và dễ viết kiểm thử. title: How to build a daily "new remote jobs" feed from public job-board APIs
author: Cedarfetch Labs
summary: You want a daily list of new remote jobs for yourself, a newsletter or a small job board. Several boards publish a JSON API or an RSS feed for exactly this. Each one comes with attribution rules and polling limits, though, and the same job often shows up on two boards. Boards with open feeds I called two of these for this post and read the terms of the rest on 2026-11-11. Re-read each board's page before you ship anything. Remote OK: https://remoteok.com/api is one JSON request. Element 0 is a legal notice, then the ~100 most recent jobs (98 today). The terms: link back to the job with a followed link (no nofollow ), name Remote OK as the source, and do not use its logo. We Work Remotely: RSS per category, for example https://weworkremotely.com/categories/remote-programming-jobs.rss (25 items today). Anyone may use the feeds; attribute the links back to the board. Remotive: https://remotive.com/api/remote-jobs , published with a 24-hour delay and meant to be polled about four times a day at most. Link back, mention Remotive, and do not forward its jobs to Google Jobs, LinkedIn Jobs, Jooble or Neuvoo. Jobicy: https://jobicy.com/api/jobs?count=100 , the last 7 days, no more than once an hour. Credit Jobicy and keep apply links on its job page. Others: 4dayweek.io allows 60 requests a minute and asks for a credit; Remote First Jobs has the same "do not forward" rule as Remotive; Arbeitnow is a free API for mostly German jobs, "do not abuse". Terms differ enough to matter. At least one board with an open API, Himalayas, forbids passing its jobs on to third parties, so I left it out. Request ( url , headers = UA ) , timeout = 30 ) as r : return r . read ( ) def remoteok ( ) : for j in json . loads ( fetch ( "https://remoteok.com/api" ) ) [ 1 : ] : # element 0 is the legal notice yield dict ( board = "remoteok" , id = j [ "id" ] , company = j [ "company" ] , title = j [ "position" ] , url = j [ "url" ] , posted = j [ "date" ] ) def weworkremotely ( ) : root = ET . fromstring ( fetch ( "https://weworkremotely.com/categories/remote-programming-jobs.rss" ) ) for it in root . iter ( "item" ) : company , _ , title = it . findtext ( "title" ) . partition ( ": " ) # "Company: Title" yield dict ( board = "weworkremotely" , id = it . findtext ( "guid" ) , company = company , title = title , url = it . findtext ( "link" ) , posted = it . findtext ( "pubDate" ) ) Output: remoteok 98 jobs; first: Mento | Strategy & Operations Coach APAC | 2026-11-11T00:00:15+00:00 weworkremotely 25 jobs; first: BDF EXPERTS | SAP Berater FI/CO (M/W/D) | Mon, 19 Oct 2026 10:01:21 +0000 We Work Remotely puts "Company: Title" in one field, so the script splits on the first ": " . Dates arrive in different formats; normalise them before you sort. Deduplicate and keep only what is new Save the first script as boards.py . This one builds a key from company and title, merges matches across boards, and remembers keys between runs. import json , os , re from boards import remoteok , weworkremotely def key ( job ) : norm = lambda s : re . sub ( r "[^a-z0-9]+" , " " , s . lower ( ) ) . strip ( ) title = re . sub ( r "\b(remote|m f d|m w d)\b" , "" , norm ( job [ "title" ] ) ) . strip ( ) return norm ( job [ "company" ] ) + "|" + title clusters = { } # key -> clusters; a cluster never holds two jobs from the same board for job in [ * remoteok ( ) , * weworkremotely ( ) ] : for cluster in clusters . setdefault ( key ( job ) , [ ] ) : if all ( j [ "board" ] != job [ "board" ] for j in cluster ) : cluster . append ( job ) break else : clusters [ key ( job ) ] . append ( [ job ] ) seen = set ( json . load ( open ( "seen.json" ) ) ) if os . path . exists ( "seen.json" ) else set ( ) for k , lists in clusters . items ( ) : if k not in seen : for c in lists : boards = "+" . join ( j [ "board" ] for j in c ) print ( f '{boards:28} {c[0]["company"]} | {c[0]["title"]} | {c[0]["url"]}' ) json . dump ( sorted ( clusters ) , open ( "seen.json" , "w" ) ) The first run printed all 122 postings. I then removed five keys from seen.json and ran it again, so those five came out as new: remoteok+weworkremotely Sanctuary Computer | Head of Technology | https://remoteOK.com/remote-jobs/remote-head-of-technology-sanctuary-computer-1137537 remoteok Addepto | Data Engineer | https://remoteOK.com/remote-jobs/remote-data-engineer-addepto-1137714 weworkremotely Airbnb | Operations Engineer, BizTech | https://weworkremotely.com/remote-jobs/airbnb-operations-engineer-biztech The first line is a real cross-post. Two different listings from the same board with the same company and title also turned up, and the script keeps those apart: two postings on one board are usually separate openings, one per region for example. Only a match across different boards is treated as a duplicate. Limits and gotchas Attribution is part of the deal. Show the source board and link to its job URL on every item. Remote OK returns URLs with a capitalised host ( remoteOK.com ); lowercase it. Messy data. Remote OK text can arrive double-encoded ( MÃ¼nchen for München ), its location is often an office city or empty, and I saw salary_min of 0 as a placeholder. Treat salaries as hints. "New" means new to the feed. Some feeds are delayed by hours or a day, and some only show a recent window, so a job that drops out of the window has not necessarily closed. Respect the windows. Cache what you fetch and poll no faster than each board says. Do not republish a board's jobs somewhere its terms forbid. No workarounds. title: Find open SAM.gov small-business set-aside bids, sorted by response deadline, in a CSV (Python, no API key)
author: Your Evenings Data
summary: Article type: How-to guide (one task: list the open SAM.gov bids set aside for small businesses, sorted by response deadline, in a CSV) Prerequisites: Python 3.9 or later with requests ( pip install requests ), and about 250 MB of free disk space. No SAM.gov API key or account: the file is public. An Apify account only if you use the hosted version at the end. Tested on: 17 November 2026, against SAM.gov's public Contract Opportunities extract dated 17 November 2026. Your business qualifies for a small-business set-aside, maybe 8(a), HUBZone, service-disabled veteran-owned (SDVOSB) or women-owned (WOSB), and you want one list of every open federal bid reserved for businesses like yours, soonest deadline first. SAM.gov publishes every active contract notice in one public CSV file that it regenerates once a day, and you don't need an API key to download it. This guide reads that file and writes the open set-aside solicitations due in the next 30 days to a CSV. The notice counts and examples in this post come from one file: https://sam.gov/api/prod/fileextractservices/v1/api/download/Contract%20Opportunities/datagov/ContractOpportunitiesFullCSV.csv?privacy=Public It was 219 MB with 72,286 notices when we ran this. It's encoded as Windows-1252 ( cp1252 ), not UTF-8, and each row carries the notice type, the set-aside code and label, the response deadline, NAICS and product/service codes, the place of performance and a link to the notice. How do I list the open set-aside bids I can respond to? The script downloads the file, keeps solicitations and combined synopsis/solicitations whose set-aside code is one of seven small-business codes, keeps the newest notice for each solicitation number, and writes those due in the next 30 days to set_aside_bids.csv . Save it as set_aside_bids.py : import csv import json from collections import Counter from datetime import datetime , timedelta , timezone from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo import requests EXTRACT = ( "https://sam.gov/api/prod/fileextractservices/v1/api/download/Contract%20Opportunities/" "datagov/ContractOpportunitiesFullCSV.csv?privacy=Public" ) SET_ASIDES = { # competitive small-business set-asides (sole-source codes left out, see gotcha 3) "SBA" : "Small business" , "SBP" : "SB partial" , "8A" : "8(a)" , "HZC" : "HUBZone" , "SDVOSBC" : "SDVOSB" , "WOSB" : "WOSB" , "EDWOSB" : "EDWOSB" , } BID_TYPES = { "Solicitation" , "Combined Synopsis/Solicitation" } DAYS_AHEAD = 30 EASTERN = ZoneInfo ( "America/New_York" ) NOW = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) # 1. Download the whole extract to disk. Open notices can be years old, so you can't stop early. with requests . get ( EXTRACT , stream = True , timeout = 600 ) as r : r . raise_for_status ( ) extract_date = r . headers . get ( "Last-Modified" ) with open ( "opportunities.csv" , "wb" ) as f : for chunk in r . iter_content ( 1 << 20 ) : f . write ( chunk ) print ( f "extract Last-Modified: {extract_date}" ) def set_aside_code ( raw ) : """Most rows hold a plain code ('SBA'); some hold a JSON list ('["SBA"]').""" raw = ( raw or "" ) . strip ( ) if raw . startswith ( "[" ) : codes = [ c for c in json . loads ( raw ) if c ] return codes [ 0 ] if codes else "" return raw def deadline ( raw ) : """Return (UTC datetime, how the time zone was known). Date-only and no-offset values are read as US Eastern.""" raw = ( raw or "" ) . strip ( ) if not raw : return None , "none" if len ( raw ) == 10 : # '2026-11-27': no time at all d = datetime . fromisoformat ( raw ) . replace ( hour = 23 , minute = 59 , tzinfo = EASTERN ) return d . astimezone ( timezone . utc ) , "date only" d = datetime . fromisoformat ( raw ) if d . tzinfo is None : # '2026-12-04T17:00:00': no offset return d . replace ( tzinfo = EASTERN ) . astimezone ( timezone . utc ) , "no offset" return d . astimezone ( timezone . utc ) , "offset given" # 2. DictReader ( f ) : seen [ "rows" ] += 1 code = set_aside_code ( row [ "SetASideCode" ] ) if row [ "Type" ] not in BID_TYPES or code not in SET_ASIDES : continue seen [ "notices" ] += 1 key = row [ "Sol#" ] . strip ( ) or row [ "NoticeId" ] if key not in latest or row [ "PostedDate" ] > latest [ key ] [ 0 ] [ "PostedDate" ] : latest [ key ] = ( row , code ) # 3. The file is sorted by posted date, newest first, so a "posted today" digest can stop early. A list of everything still open can't: 682 of the 2,657 solicitations were posted more than seven days before the run, and the oldest on 14 November 2025. Keep the newest notice per solicitation number. An amendment is posted as a new notice under the same number. Of 23,383 solicitation numbers on bid notices, 6,066 had more than one notice, 3,775 of those with different deadlines across their notices and 447 with different set-aside codes. Without collapsing them you'd get 3,292 rows instead of 2,657. Collapse first and filter by date second: done the other way round, 11 solicitations stayed on the list with an old notice's deadline, even though their newest notice had moved the deadline past the 30-day window or into the past. Bid notices only. The file also holds 11,540 award notices plus presolicitations, sources sought and special notices. Those can be worth watching, but you can't submit a bid against most of them yet. No contact columns. Each row also has a primary and a secondary point of contact, with name, email and phone. The script doesn't copy them, so the CSV holds notice data only. What should I check before I trust the list? Most notices have no set-aside code at all. 41,297 of the 72,286 rows had an empty SetASideCode and 5,864 had NONE . Filter on the codes you want, and don't read an empty code as a set-aside. Some codes are JSON lists. 201 rows, all from one department, held ["SBA"] (189) or [""] (12) in the code column with an empty label. None of them was due in our 30-day window, but a plain == "SBA" test skips them without telling you. The script unwraps the list. Sole-source codes aren't open competitions. 8AN , SDVOSBS , HZS and WOSBSS (41, 83, 18 and 19 bid notices here) are the sole-source versions of the 8(a), SDVOSB, HUBZone and WOSB codes. The script leaves them out; add them to SET_ASIDES if you want to see them. Deadlines come in four shapes. Across the file, 51,272 deadlines had a UTC offset, 11,958 were a date with no time, 702 had a time but no offset and 8,354 were empty. In our 2,657 rows, 1,787 were date only and 8 had a time but no offset. Most date-only deadlines are on combined synopsis/solicitations (11,714 of the 11,958). The script reads a date-only deadline as 23:59 US Eastern on that date and a time with no offset as US Eastern. That's our assumption, not SAM.gov's, and a rough one: only 37,601 of the 51,272 deadlines with an offset (73%) used -05:00 or -04:00 , the offsets US Eastern uses. So the CSV keeps the original text in deadline_as_posted and says which case applied in deadline_tz . Check the notice before you plan around a date-only deadline or one with no offset. Don't sort the deadline text. The offsets ranged from -10:00 to +13:00 (26 different ones), because notices are posted from many time zones, overseas places of performance included. Sorted as text, 2,580 of the 2,657 rows land in a different position from the real order. For example, 2026-11-17T10:00:00-08:00 (18:00 UTC) sorts before 2026-11-17T11:00:00-05:00 (16:00 UTC). Convert to UTC first, as the script does. Place of performance is often empty. 2,096 of the 2,657 rows had no state. If you filter by state, decide what to do with those rows instead of dropping them silently. The file is about a day behind. Ours was dated 04:30 GMT on 17 November, so notices posted or amended after that weren't in it. Check Last-Modified and the notice page on SAM.gov before you bid. To change the list, edit SET_ASIDES , BID_TYPES (add "Sources Sought" for early market research notices) or DAYS_AHEAD , or add a NAICS test on row["NaicsCode"] . The hosted version (Disclosure: we built this) We built an Apify Actor, SAM.gov Scraper: Government Contracts, Bids & Federal Grants , that reads the same public extract on every run, so it needs no SAM.gov key either. Set opportunityType to contracts and list codes in setAsideTypes . It reads list-style codes such as ["SBA"] (gotcha 2) as the plain code, so they match your filter and come back as SBA ; a notice with several codes comes back as, for example, SBA,8A and matches a filter on any of them, and an empty list counts as no code. A date-only deadline comes back as the date itself (for example 2026-11-27 ) with responseDeadlineHasTime: false , and a deadline with a time comes back with responseDeadlineHasTime: true : as a UTC timestamp when SAM.gov gives an offset or the notice text states the zone, otherwise as the local time SAM.gov gave with no Z, and responseDeadlineTimeZoneBasis says which. All 8 no-offset deadlines in our 2,657 rows would come back as local times, marked unknown . The Actor doesn't sort by deadline, because date-only values and timestamps have to be converted to one form first. dueAfter keeps notices whose deadline falls on or after a date, compared by calendar date, and leaves out notices with no deadline when you set it. Two things it still doesn't do. It returns one row per notice, so amendments under one solicitation number come back as separate rows: keep one row per solicitationNumber , and check the notice pages when two notices share the newest date (1,387 solicitations in the file have two or more notices on the same newest date). The 'Solicitation' filter also returns presolicitations and combined synopsis/solicitations, so drop Presolicitation rows if you only want bids. The default window is notices posted in the last seven days, so set postedSince to reach older open notices. It adds a free warning row when the extract is more than 36 hours old or empty, contact fields are off by default, and monitor mode returns only notices it hasn't returned before. It's pay per event, charged per opportunity row returned; the prices are on the Actor's Pricing tab. For example (not run for this post): { "opportunityType" : "contracts" , "setAsideTypes" : [ "SBA" , "SBP" , "8A" , "HZC" , "SDVOSBC" , "WOSB" , "EDWOSB" ] , "samNoticeTypes" : [ "Solicitation" ] , "postedSince" : "2025-01-01" , "dueAfter" : "2026-11-17" , "maxResults" : 0 } SAM.gov Scraper on Apify Data: SAM.gov Contract Opportunities public extract (Data Services), file dated 17 November 2026, read 17 November 2026. Notices are as posted by the agencies. This post and the Actor are not affiliated with or endorsed by SAM.gov, the U.S. General Services Administration or any agency named. Your Evenings

title: Site Works for Me but Not for Them: A 5-Step Debugging Checklist
author: Baleeghuddin shaikh
summary: A client messages you: "The site is down." You open it, and it loads perfectly. You try your phone, and it works there too. So who is right? Usually both. "Works for me" and "down for them" can both be true at the same time, because the path from their browser to your server is not the same as yours. Different DNS resolvers, different caches, different networks, different devices. This is the checklist I run through, in order. Each step rules out a whole category of problems. Step 1: Check from outside your own network Your browser is the worst witness. It has cached DNS, cached redirects, maybe a cached HSTS policy, and it is sitting on your network. Start with an external check that requests the page from a different location: Or use an online website status checker . If the external check also fails, the site really is down. If it succeeds, keep going. The problem is somewhere between them and you. Step 2: Compare DNS answers If you recently changed hosting or DNS records, different resolvers may still be returning different answers. Their ISP's resolver may hold the old IP for the length of the old TTL. If those two disagree, or disagree with your authoritative nameserver, that is your answer. Wait out the TTL, or ask the user to flush their DNS. A DNS lookup tool shows what public resolvers return without touching your local cache. Step 3: Check the SSL certificate chain This is the one that hides best. If your server sends its certificate but not the intermediate certificate, most desktop browsers quietly fetch the missing piece and show a padlock. Many mobile browsers, older devices and command-line tools do not, and they show a security warning instead. So the site works on your laptop and fails on their phone. Count the certificates in the output. If you only see one, the chain is incomplete. With Let's Encrypt, the fix is almost always pointing your server at fullchain.pem instead of cert.pem . An SSL checker shows the full chain from outside your network. Step 4: Follow the redirects Redirect rules can behave differently depending on cookies, location, device or whether the visitor typed www . A user stuck in ERR_TOO_MANY_REDIRECTS will see a broken site while yours loads fine. This shows every hop and its status code. More than one or two hops, or the same URL appearing twice, means a rule needs fixing. A redirect checker does the same from outside your network. Step 5: Test the port from outside If the page times out for them, a firewall may be dropping traffic from their network or region. Testing from your own machine bypasses that firewall, so it proves nothing. Run that from another network, or use an external open port checker . A refused connection means the service is not listening. A timeout means something is silently dropping the packets. The Short Version When a site works for you but not for someone else, do not start with the server logs. Start by checking the path: an external status check, then DNS answers from public resolvers, then the certificate chain, then the redirect chain, then the port from outside. One of those five almost always explains the difference. I keep free versions of all of these checks at Web Tools Realm . No sign-up, and they run from the server side, so the results are not affected by your browser's cache.

title: Optimizely: malware en su script afectó a 178 empresas, según un reporte
author: lu1tr0n
summary: El 16 de noviembre de 2026, alguien escribió código malicioso en el campo de JavaScript personalizado de cientos de proyectos de Optimizely y convirtió una herramienta de A/B testing en un canal de distribución de malware. La firma de seguridad Report URI documentó el ataque y contó 178 organizaciones afectadas, entre ellas Zoom, la BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger y Peacock. Optimizely Web funciona así: cada cliente carga un snippet de JavaScript desde el CDN de la empresa, por ejemplo cdn.optimizely.com/js/6395285578973184.js , y ese archivo decide qué variante de una página mostrarle a cada visitante. El snippet incluye un campo opcional llamado Project JavaScript : código propio que el cliente escribe desde su panel de Optimizely y que corre en cada carga de página. El atacante escribió el suyo ahí, dejó el resto del snippet intacto y nunca tocó el certificado ni la infraestructura del CDN. Por eso cada sitio afectado seguía sirviendo el malware desde un dominio y un certificado que ya consideraba de confianza, según el reporte de Report URI . Qué hacía el script en cada visita El payload, un archivo llamado track.js , cumplía varias funciones a la vez y se reescribió 26 veces durante el día: el atacante agregaba funciones y billeteras nuevas, pero nunca quitó ninguna, según el seguimiento de Report URI. La función más directa buscaba direcciones de criptomonedas (BTC, ETH y cadenas EVM, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash y Dogecoin) en el texto de la página, en formularios y en el portapapeles, validaba el checksum para asegurarse de que fuera una dirección real y la reemplazaba por una del atacante. El mismo script robaba datos de tarjetas de pago, cookies y capturas de pantalla. En visitantes de iPhone y iPad con iOS 18.6 o anterior, inyectaba un iframe que entregaba los kits de exploits conocidos como Coruna y DarkSword . Report URI confirmó transacciones de criptomonedas ya consumadas hacia las billeteras del atacante. El atacante usó tres variantes del cargador para no depender de un solo método: una etiqueta script directa a 1688360.cc/track.js en la mayoría de los snippets, la misma URL escondida en base64 dentro de un atob() para que una búsqueda simple del dominio no la encontrara, y una copia completa del payload en línea que corre con eval si el dominio 1688360.cc está bloqueado. Esa última variante vuelve inútil bloquear solo el dominio: el código ya está dentro de la página. flowchart TD A [ "Atacante" ] --> B [ "Campo Project JavaScript en el panel de Optimizely" ] B --> C [ "Snippet servido desde cdn.optimizely.com" ] C --> D [ "Navegador del visitante" ] D --> E [ "track.js: swap de wallets y robo de tarjetas" ] D --> F [ "iOS 18.6 o anterior: iframe con Coruna y DarkSword" ] Cronología del ataque a Optimizely: de un snippet limpio a 186 infectados La primera inyección confirmada en un snippet de Optimizely ocurrió a las 04:21 UTC del 16 de noviembre, en el código que carga la BBC; a las 02:21 esa misma copia todavía estaba limpia. Minutos después se emitieron los certificados del dominio 1688360.cc , registrado a las 05:23, y a las 08:10 apareció la primera versión de track.js . El robo de criptomonedas hacia los exchanges del atacante quedó registrado a las 13:03 y el robo de tarjetas se agregó a las 13:43. La limpieza masiva empezó recién entre las 20:40 y las 21:10 UTC: Ledger a las 20:41, Smartsheet a las 20:56 y la BBC a las 21:07. A las 21:52 solo quedaba 1 de 188 snippets todavía infectado (el de TalkTalk), frente a 169 una hora antes, según el seguimiento de Report URI . Un detalle que una lectura rápida del caso suele dejar afuera: el snippet de Smartsheet se limpió una vez y volvió a infectarse con la versión del cargador en base64, lo que indica que quien escribía el código todavía tenía acceso durante el incidente, no solo en el momento inicial. Qué significa para vos si tu sitio usa herramientas de experimentación Si tu equipo de producto o marketing usa Optimizely, o cualquier plataforma que permita escribir JavaScript propio dentro de un snippet de terceros, revisá hoy quién tiene permiso de escritura en ese proyecto. El ataque no rompió el CDN de Optimizely: entró por un acceso a la configuración de clientes concretos. Si tu snippet se sirve desde tu propio dominio como proxy, como hacían algunas víctimas con direcciones del tipo opt.scheels.com , seguís expuesto igual, porque el contenido viene del mismo proyecto de Optimizely. La segunda acción es técnica: activar una Content Security Policy en modo de aplicación ( enforce , no solo report-only ) que limite a qué dominios puede conectarse el script de tu proveedor de experimentación. Una CSP correcta no habría bloqueado el snippet en sí, porque seguía viniendo de cdn.optimizely.com , pero sí habría cortado la conexión saliente hacia 1688360.cc si ese dominio no estaba en la lista blanca. Report URI señala justamente eso: su monitoreo de cambios inesperados en JavaScript confiable habría mostrado la alteración del snippet aunque viniera de un dominio de confianza. ⚠️ Ojo: si tu proyecto de Optimizely sirve el snippet desde un dominio propio como proxy, el ataque te afecta igual que a quien lo carga directo desde cdn.optimizely.com: el contenido es el mismo. 178 organizaciones corrieron el mismo script malicioso el 16 de noviembre de 2026. Optimizely frente a LaunchDarkly, Split y Statsig Optimizely Web no es la única forma de decidir qué versión de una página ve cada usuario. LaunchDarkly y Statsig resuelven feature flags y experimentos evaluando reglas dentro de un SDK que corre en el propio código del cliente, sin un campo abierto para pegar JavaScript arbitrario que el proveedor sirva por vos. Split , ahora parte de Harness, sigue un modelo parecido: el cliente decide qué variante mostrar con su propio código y la plataforma solo entrega la configuración. La diferencia no es que esas alternativas sean inmunes a un compromiso (cualquier SDK de terceros es una superficie de ataque), sino que ninguna ofrece, por diseño, un campo tipo Project JavaScript donde una sola cuenta con acceso al panel puede escribir código que se ejecuta sin revisión en cada carga de página de cientos de clientes distintos. Ese campo es justamente lo que el atacante usó en Optimizely. Qué dice la comunidad En la discusión de Hacker News sobre el caso, el usuario kursus recordó que, antes de que existiera el concepto de tag manager, era común que los sitios cargaran a ciegas un archivo JS del servidor de su proveedor de tracking, mantenido por el equipo de ese proveedor y no por el sitio. Para kursus, la práctica de confiar sin revisar un script de terceros no es nueva, solo cambió de nombre. Otro comentario, de dboreham , especula que algunos sitios grandes como CNN podrían separar sus páginas de pago del script de marketing y tracking, aunque aclara que no hay confirmación de que ese fuera el caso en este ataque. Los límites de la respuesta de Optimizely Optimizely no explicó públicamente cómo el atacante obtuvo acceso de escritura a tantos proyectos de clientes sin relación entre sí. Pudo ser un sistema interno comprometido, una credencial con acceso cruzado entre cuentas, o algo distinto que la empresa todavía no detalla. Report URI aclaró que no fue un ataque de envenenamiento de caché del CDN: el CDN sirvió exactamente el contenido que cada proyecto tenía configurado. La limpieza fue rápida una vez detectada, de 169 snippets infectados a 1 en menos de una hora, pero no cierra el problema de fondo. Si el acceso llegó por una credencial robada o un sistema interno de Optimizely, nada impide una reinfección hasta que la empresa confirme y corrija esa vía. Además, el modo del payload que corre con eval vuelve relevante otro detalle de la CSP: una política que todavía permite unsafe-eval no habría bloqueado esa copia inline, solo las dos versiones que dependían de cargar un script externo desde 1688360.cc . Quitar unsafe-eval de la CSP es más difícil que agregar un dominio a una lista negra, pero es la única defensa real contra ese tercer modo. Referencias Report URI: World's Largest Brands Infected With Malware Via Optimizely : cronología completa del ataque, lista de 178 organizaciones afectadas y mecanismo de inyección en el campo Project JavaScript.- Report URI : detalle técnico del payload track.js, con el robo de criptomonedas, el skimming de tarjetas y la entrega de los kits de exploits Coruna y DarkSword en iOS.- Report URI : recomendación de monitoreo de cambios en JavaScript confiable y uso de CSP en modo de aplicación para mitigar ataques similares.- Hacker News : discusión de la comunidad sobre el incidente y sus implicancias para sitios que cargan scripts de terceros. Seguimos el tema en @programacion .
