title: Building an AI-Simulated Client for Counselling Training: Lessons From PraxisAI
author: ThinkShift Consulting
summary: An AI-simulated client is an AI-powered character that allows trainees to practise realistic counselling conversations without requiring a human role-play partner for every session. The system can respond to what the trainee says, maintain a scenario, adapt the conversation and provide structured feedback after the session. That is the idea behind PraxisAI , an AI human-skills simulation and assessment platform built by ThinkShift. Trainee counsellors can practise conversations with AI clients through voice, avatar and chat, with sessions evaluated against defined competencies. The interesting engineering challenge isn't simply making an AI that can talk. It is making an AI that can stay inside a scenario, behave consistently, create a useful training experience and turn a conversation into measurable feedback. That became the core problem we explored while building PraxisAI. What Is an AI-Simulated Client? An AI-simulated client is a virtual client powered by AI for training or role-play. Instead of following a fixed dialogue tree, the simulated client can respond dynamically to the trainee's questions and statements. This makes the interaction less predictable than traditional scripted practice. For counselling training, that distinction matters. A trainee shouldn't only practise asking a predefined list of questions. They need to experience what happens when a conversation changes direction, when a client gives an unexpected answer, or when important information emerges gradually. Recent research has started evaluating generative AI in exactly this role. Studies have found that AI can provide a flexible environment for practising counselling skills, while also identifying limitations around emotional nuance, authenticity, cultural dynamics and overly agreeable responses. So the product challenge becomes: How do you make an AI conversation useful for learning, rather than simply interesting to interact with? Why Use AI for Counselling Role-Play? Traditional role-play is valuable, but it has practical limitations. Two students need to be available at the same time. One person has to play the client. The scenario may change depending on the person playing the role. And repeating the same exercise many times isn't always easy. An AI client introduces another option. A trainee can practise a scenario, review the interaction, try again and compare the results. That creates a learning loop: Practice → Conversation → Feedback → Reflection → Practice again The value is not that AI replaces a supervisor or a human client. The value is that it can create additional opportunities to practise between structured teaching and real-world experience. Research published in 2025 similarly found that AI-simulated counselling sessions could offer a psychologically safer and flexible environment for practice, while concluding that AI should supplement rather than replace live training. The Real Challenge: Making the Client Feel Consistent A generic chatbot can answer questions. A useful training simulator needs to do more. Imagine a scenario where a client is initially reluctant to discuss a particular problem. If the trainee asks an open-ended question, the client might gradually reveal more. If the trainee interrupts or asks a leading question, the client might respond differently. If the trainee demonstrates empathy and creates space, the conversation may develop in another direction. The system therefore needs to maintain more than conversational fluency. It needs to maintain scenario state . That means keeping track of things such as: the client's background the scenario and presenting concern information already disclosed information that has not yet been disclosed the client's conversational behaviour the training objective the counselling approach being practised the progression of the conversation Without this context, an AI client can quickly start behaving like a generic assistant. And that breaks the simulation. Designing Realistic AI Role-Play Realism doesn't mean making the AI sound human in every sentence. In a training environment, realism means creating behaviour that makes sense within the scenario . A simulated client may: hesitate before answering avoid a subject provide incomplete information change their level of openness ask the trainee a question react differently to different counselling approaches reveal information progressively misunderstand something become more comfortable as the conversation develops These behaviours create opportunities for the trainee to practise actual communication skills. Research into AI-simulated counselling has identified a similar challenge: AI can produce convincing interactions, but overly idealised responses, limited emotional nuance and missing non-verbal cues can reduce authenticity. That means realism has to be treated as a product design problem , not just an LLM prompt. From AI Conversation to Training Simulation This was one of the biggest distinctions in building PraxisAI. A chatbot answers a user's message. A training simulator has a learning objective . Those are very different systems. For example, the objective might be to help a trainee practise reflective listening. The system then needs to evaluate the conversation against that competency rather than simply deciding whether the final answer sounded good. This creates a second layer around the AI conversation: AI client → conversation → competency evaluation → feedback That second layer is where the product becomes a training system. Why Feedback Matters A realistic conversation is useful. A realistic conversation followed by useful feedback is much more useful. After a practice session, trainees need to understand what happened. Instead of receiving a generic score such as: "Good job — 8/10." the feedback should connect the assessment to the actual interaction. For example: Where did the trainee demonstrate a specific competency? Which response could have been handled differently? Did the trainee ask too many questions? Did they reflect what the client was saying? Did they move too quickly through an important disclosure? What could they try differently in the next session? This creates a connection between what happened and what to practise next . PraxisAI is designed around this assessment layer, with sessions evaluated against competencies rather than treating the conversation as an isolated chatbot interaction. Designing Competency-Based Assessment One of the interesting product challenges is that counselling isn't one single skill. Different approaches can emphasise different techniques and competencies. So an assessment system needs to understand the context in which a conversation is taking place. That means the evaluation layer needs to consider: Scenario + approach + conversation + competency framework rather than: Conversation + generic AI score This is important because the same response could be appropriate in one context and less useful in another. The assessment therefore becomes part of the product architecture, not something added after the AI conversation has been built. Practice and Assessment Are Different Modes Another useful distinction is between practice and assessment . During practice, the trainee is learning. They may want guidance, feedback and opportunities to repeat a scenario. During assessment, the objective is different: the trainee should demonstrate their skills with less intervention. Separating these experiences makes the product more useful because the system is supporting two different user goals. This is a broader lesson for AI product development: Don't build one AI experience and expect it to serve every stage of the user's journey. The AI behaviour, interface and evaluation system should change according to what the user is trying to accomplish. Building for Voice, Avatar and Chat PraxisAI is designed around multiple interaction formats, including voice, avatar and chat. This creates another product consideration. Text-based interaction gives the system a clean representation of the conversation. Voice introduces additional dimensions such as: pacing pauses tone speaking behaviour turn-taking An avatar adds another visual layer to the experience. The underlying training objective, however, should remain consistent. The interface can change without losing the core learning loop: Interact → Evaluate → Understand → Improve That separation between the interaction layer and the learning layer is useful when designing AI training products. What We Learned About AI Simulation 1. A prompt is not a product It is easy to demonstrate an AI role-play by writing a detailed prompt. Building a reliable product around that interaction is much harder. You need scenario management, user flows, evaluation logic, feedback, persistence and a clear learning objective. 2. Realism needs boundaries Giving an AI complete freedom doesn't necessarily produce the best simulation. Training scenarios need constraints. The AI should have enough freedom to create natural conversations while remaining consistent with the scenario and learning objective. 3. Evaluation needs structure If every assessment is generated from scratch, results can become inconsistent. A useful training system needs defined competencies and a consistent evaluation framework. The AI can then interpret the conversation within those boundaries. 4. The conversation is only one part of the experience The most visible part of an AI simulator is the conversation. But the less visible parts, scenario setup, evaluation, feedback and progress tracking, may create much of the product's actual value. 5. AI should support human learning This is perhaps the most important lesson. AI simulation can create more practice opportunities, but it doesn't reproduce everything that happens in a real human interaction. Current research continues to identify limitations around emotional depth, authenticity, cultural sensitivity and non-verbal communication. So the right goal isn't: "Replace human counselling practice with AI." It's: "Use AI to make structured practice more accessible and repeatable." Building an AI Product in Dubai PraxisAI is one example of the type of AI product development we work on at ThinkShift . ThinkShift is based in Dubai and focuses on building working products that can be tested with real users rather than spending months building around assumptions. That approach influenced how we thought about PraxisAI. Instead of asking: "How can we build a chatbot for counsellors?" the more useful question was: "What would make AI genuinely useful for someone learning counselling skills?" That change in framing affected the product. The AI conversation became one component. The scenario became another. The competency framework became another. And the feedback loop connected everything together. That is an important distinction when building AI products in Dubai—or anywhere else. The technology is only one part of the product. The real work is connecting the technology to a measurable user problem. Can AI Replace Human Role-Play? No. AI-simulated clients should be considered a supplement to human-led training , not a replacement for supervisors, educators or real human interaction. Research from 2025 found promising results for AI-assisted counselling practice, including improvements in trainee confidence and reductions in anxiety in one study, but the researchers also emphasised the need for thoughtful integration and further research. Human interaction still brings qualities that AI cannot perfectly reproduce: emotional complexity non-verbal communication cultural context professional judgement unpredictable behaviour genuine interpersonal relationships AI can provide another layer of practice. It shouldn't pretend to be the complete training environment. Frequently Asked Questions What is an AI-simulated client? An AI-simulated client is an AI-powered character designed to interact with a trainee in a practice scenario. It can respond dynamically to the trainee while maintaining the context and objectives of the scenario. How does AI role-play training work? AI role-play training places a learner inside a simulated conversation with an AI character. The AI responds according to the scenario, while the learner practises specific skills. The interaction can then be reviewed and evaluated. Can AI simulate a client for counselling practice? Yes. Recent research has evaluated generative AI as a simulated client for counselling role-play and found potential value as a supplementary training tool. However, researchers have also identified limitations involving realism, emotional nuance and cultural context. What is an AI conversation simulator? An AI conversation simulator is a system that generates interactive conversations for training, practice or assessment. Unlike a fixed script, it can respond dynamically to what the user says. What are the benefits of AI-simulated client training? The main benefits include repeatable practice, flexible access to scenarios, lower-pressure practice environments and structured feedback. It can give trainees additional opportunities to practise before working with real people. How does AI provide feedback on counselling practice? An AI training system can analyse a conversation against predefined competencies and identify specific moments that demonstrate or miss those competencies. The feedback can then explain what happened and suggest areas for improvement. Can AI role-play create realistic client scenarios? It can create increasingly realistic scenarios, but realism depends on scenario design, context, prompting and evaluation. Current research still identifies limitations in emotional nuance, cultural responsiveness and non-verbal communication. What are the limitations of AI counselling simulations? AI simulations can struggle with subtle emotions, cultural context, non-verbal signals and the unpredictability of genuine human interactions. They should therefore be used with appropriate educational guidance and human oversight. Can AI replace human role-play in counselling training? No. AI can supplement role-play by providing additional practice opportunities, but it should not replace human supervision, education or real-world interpersonal experience. Final Thoughts Building an AI-simulated client taught us that the difficult part isn't making AI talk. The difficult part is making the conversation useful . For a training product, that means thinking beyond the model: Scenario → Interaction → Competency → Assessment → Feedback → Improvement Once those pieces work together, an AI conversation stops being just a demonstration of generative AI. It becomes a tool for structured practice. And that is the direction we are exploring with PraxisAI : using applied AI to help people practise important human skills more often, receive better feedback and become more prepared for real-world interactions.

title: A reader found a hole in our AI inbox. Postgres closes it now
author: Viacheslav Bobok
summary: In my last post I wrote about how our AI assistant can write to exactly one table . Claude, connected to Reperline over MCP, can only insert rows into pending_changes . A person approves or rejects each one in an inbox, and apply_pending_change writes the real tables with the approver's own rights. I ended that post with "the inbox is where the real control happens". In the comments, Mike Johnstone pointed out that the inbox had a hole of its own: A proposal can go stale in the inbox too. If someone changes a milestone before approval, the reviewer may be looking at a diff against an old value. He was right, and the bug was worse than a confusing screen. This post is the fix, migration 064. How the bug looked on a real site A milestone proposal carries an absolute value, not a delta: { "milestone_id" : "..." , "progress" : 65 , "note" : "from the site report photos" } Here is the sequence that broke it: The milestone is at 55%. Claude reads a site report and proposes 65%. The proposal waits in the inbox over lunch. Meanwhile the site manager walks the floor and records 70% from Telegram. The project manager opens the inbox, sees "55% to 65%", which looks reasonable, and clicks Approve. apply_pending_change writes 65%. Progress just went down by five points. Our normal entry path refuses to lower progress without a note explaining why, but that rule lived in the application function that records a fact from the UI and Telegram. The approval path wrote the journal directly, so the drop went in silently. Nobody did anything wrong, and the database accepted a value that was already false when it was approved. The grants from the first post did their job. Claude still wrote nothing by itself. A person approved a stale diff, and the approval was the hole. Option one: compare in the UI The quick fix is to show the current value next to the proposal and hope the reviewer notices. We do show it now, but a check that lives only on the screen is the same kind of promise the first post was about avoiding. Another client, a script or a second tab can still approve. The check had to be inside apply_pending_change , in the same transaction as the write. What exactly is "the base"? Mike suggested storing the base row version with the proposal. The idea is right; choosing which version took most of the work. A row version such as xmin . It changes on any update of the milestone row, including a renamed milestone or a corrected planned date. Every unrelated edit would strand every open proposal. The current progress value alone. It misses the case 70 → 55 → 70: someone records a drop, then measures again and records 70. The value is back where it was, but two facts were entered that the proposal never saw. The reviewer should look again. The id or timestamp of the latest journal row. Facts can be back dated ( reported_at is when the work was measured, not when it was typed), so "latest by reported_at" misses a late entry of an older measurement. created_at is the transaction start time, so rows inserted in one transaction tie, and a transaction that started earlier can commit later. What we used: the number of journal rows plus the progress value. Every fact for a milestone is a new row in milestone_updates , and a trigger moves milestones.progress on every insert. So the count changes exactly when progress may have changed, regardless of dates. Comparing progress as well covers the remaining blind spot (a delete plus an insert keeps the count). Our app never deletes a fact, but the role technically still holds DELETE , so we did not want to rely on that. Stamping the base: the client does not get a say If Claude sent the base, a prompt could make it send whatever value makes the check pass. So the base is stamped by a BEFORE INSERT trigger, and anything the client put in those keys is overwritten: create function stamp_proposal_base ( ) returns trigger language plpgsql as $$ declare v_progress int ; v_facts bigint ; begin if new . kind <> 'milestone_update' or jsonb_typeof ( new . payload ) <> 'object' then return new ; end if ; -- one statement, one snapshot: progress and count describe the same moment select m . progress , ( select count (*) from milestone_updates u where u.milestone_id = m.id and u.org_id = m.org_id) into v_progress, v_facts from milestones m where m.id = nullif(new.payload->>'milestone_id', '')::uuid and m.org_id = new.org_id; new.payload := new.payload || jsonb_build_object('base_progress', v_progress, 'base_facts', v_facts); return new; end $$; create trigger b_stamp_base before insert on pending_changes for each row execute function stamp_proposal_base(); Two details: The function is SECURITY INVOKER , so it reads with the proposer's row level security. If the proposer cannot see the milestone, the base is stamped as null, and a null base never matches, so such a proposal can never be approved. The trigger name starts with b_ on purpose. Postgres fires BEFORE triggers in name order, and our a_guard_closed trigger, which refuses changes to a closed phase, has to run first. Checking it: lock first, then read In apply_pending_change the milestone branch now does this before writing: -- lock first, then read in a new statement perform 1 from milestones where id = ( pl ->> 'milestone_id' ) :: uuid and org_id = pc . org_id for update ; select m . progress , ( select count (*) from milestone_updates u where u.milestone_id = m.id and u.org_id = m.org_id) into cur_progress, cur_facts from milestones m where m.id = (pl->>'milestone_id')::uuid and m.org_id = pc.org_id; if (cur_facts, cur_progress) is distinct from ((pl->>'base_facts')::bigint, (pl->>'base_progress')::int) then raise exception 'proposal_stale'; end if; The split into two statements matters. Under READ COMMITTED , each statement inside a PL/pgSQL function gets a fresh snapshot. If the count ran in the same statement as the lock, it could use a snapshot taken before the lock was granted. A fact that committed while we were waiting would be missing from the count, and we would approve over it. The lock also closes the window from the other side. Inserting a fact takes a KEY SHARE lock on the milestone (the foreign key) and the trigger then updates the row, so no fact can land between our check and our own journal insert. is distinct from instead of <> matters too: it treats null as a value, so a null base never compares equal to anything. Rejecting is never checked. A stale proposal can always be thrown away; it just cannot be approved. The inbox The UI shows the same thing the database enforces. A stale proposal gets a red notice ("It was 55% when proposed. A fact was entered since, so the proposal can only be rejected.") and a disabled Approve button. That is a display hint only. The function refuses on its own, and the error key proposal_stale is translated for anyone who reaches it some other way. Proposals that were already waiting when the migration ran were backfilled with the current state, so the existing inbox was not stranded by the upgrade. The test that made me trust it Each case runs against a real Postgres, with Claude's role filing the proposal: nothing changed since the proposal: approval works; a fact after the proposal: approval refused, and the site fact stands; 70 → 55 → 70: refused, because the count moved; rejecting a stale proposal still works; Claude sends base_progress: 10, base_facts: 99 : both are overwritten by the trigger; two open proposals for one milestone: approving one makes the other stale; lock order: a second connection inserts a fact and holds the transaction open. The approval starts and the test polls pg_locks until it sees the approval waiting. Then the fact commits, and the approval must fail with proposal_stale . That last one is the case that is easiest to get wrong and hardest to see in review, so it is the one I would not ship without. What I take from this The first post was about making sure the AI cannot write. This one is about the next layer: a person approving is only meaningful if they approve against the data as it is now. Optimistic concurrency is an old idea; the work was in choosing a version marker that changes when it should and only then, and in making the stamp something the proposer cannot fake. And thanks to Mike. A comment section that finds a real bug in a week is worth more than any launch post. If you are building an approval inbox for an AI agent: store what the proposal was based on, stamp it on the server, and check it under a lock in the same transaction that writes.

title: Your AI agent's shared memory leaks data it was never given — here's a 5-minute test
author: vsangaraju
summary: A Finance agent computes average income by region and caches it. A second agent derives "high-income regions are growing fastest" from that cached figure and stores it too. A Marketing agent asks about regional growth — and gets an answer built from salary data it was never allowed to see. No one attacked anything. No permissions were misconfigured. The memory did exactly what it was designed to do: serve cached results to agents that can search the same space. The leak is structural. Whenever agents share memory and build on each other's cached work, restricted information flows into new records that no longer name their source. I measured it in my IEEE Access paper: 18.8–25.5% of cross-team retrievals leaked restricted columns against a content-gated baseline. In mem0, plain memory leaked derived content in 71% of queries. Test your own memory in 5 minutes As one agent, write a record built from a restricted source. As a second agent, write a summary of that record. As a third agent without access to the source, search for the summary's topic. If the summary comes back, your memory has the derived-data leak. The check works on any shared agent memory — mem0, a Postgres store, a LangChain retriever, anything that caches results across agents. The fix: derivation gating Every stored result carries the lineage of how it was computed, closed over everything it was built from. A read succeeds only if the requester may see every sensitive input in that lineage. Missing lineage fails closed. It's a simple rule, and it works: across four synthetic benchmarks, the gate removed the leak entirely while keeping most of the reuse benefit. Leak rate Reuse kept Content-gated baseline 18.8–25.5% 95.8% Derivation-gated 0% 81.6–82.6% In the mem0 benchmark, plain mem0 leaked in 71.2% of queries; the gate leaked in none, with Recall@10 of 0.999 for entitled users. The limits, stated plainly All four benchmarks are synthetic. The guarantee depends on complete lineage — when only 90% of derivation edges were recorded, 11.7% of queries still leaked. And the leak rate reaches zero partly by construction: the gate checks the same labels the leak metric counts. The benchmarks show the mechanism is sound and affordable on these workloads; they are not production estimates. The gate also doesn't stop inference from content — a paraphrase of restricted data with no declared source is outside what lineage can see. The whitepaper and the code I wrote up the full picture — the mechanism, a reference architecture, and open-source implementations — as a whitepaper: Derivation-Gated Memory for AI Agents , doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24316521 . The implementations are all open source (MIT): amu-governance — the core model, policy registry, and SQL lineage extraction ( GitHub ) amu-pgvector — PostgreSQL + pgvector, enforced by row-level security ( GitHub ) langchain-amu — AMUVectorStore, listed in LangChain's integration docs ( GitHub ) amu-pgvector-mcp — MCP server, one per agent role ( GitHub ) amu-mem0 — a wrapper around mem0 reads ( GitHub ) Prefer the storage-level gate wherever memory lives in Postgres — one policy covers raw SQL, Python, LangChain, and MCP. Use the wrapper when the memory library owns the store. The underlying research is Lineage-Aware Memory Governance (Sangaraju & Vissa, IEEE Access, vol. 14, 2026). Try the check If you run shared memory for agents over governed data, run the five-minute check and see what comes back. If your memory leaks, I'd like to hear about it — and if the gate fixes it, I'd like to hear that too. Venkata M Sangaraju is a Sr Database Engineer working on access governance for analytics and AI systems. This is independent open-source work, not a publication of his employer.

title: x402 TypeScript Tutorial: Let Your AI Agent Pay Per Call for Web Search (Node.js)
author: AgentSearch
summary: If you build agents in TypeScript, you've probably hit the same wall every time you add a web tool: sign up, verify an email, copy an API key into .env , pick a plan. Then do it again for the next tool. x402 removes that step. The server answers an unpaid request with HTTP 402 Payment Required and a machine-readable price. Your client signs a small USDC payment, retries, and gets the answer. There's no account, no key and no monthly plan, so an agent can pay for exactly the calls it makes. This guide builds that in Node.js with TypeScript, step by step: Read a live 402 price for free, with plain fetch . Pay per call with @x402/fetch . Wrap search and page reads as agent tools with a hard budget. Run them in a tool-calling loop with the OpenAI Node SDK. The API is AgentSearch's direct x402 API at api.agentsearchhq.com , on Base mainnet. The same code works for any x402 v2 seller. What it costs Live prices from GET https://api.agentsearchhq.com/x402/v1/pricing : Endpoint What it does Price per call POST /x402/v1/search Live web search, ranked results as JSON $0.003 POST /x402/v1/extract Any public URL to clean markdown $0.002 POST /x402/v1/search_and_read Search plus the top pages as markdown, one call $0.005 POST /x402/v1/render JavaScript-heavy pages in headless Chromium see Render Payments are USDC on Base, x402 v2 exact scheme, settled through the Coinbase CDP facilitator. Failed and empty calls are never settled: payment is verified first and only settled after a usable answer. A typical "search once, read two pages" question costs $0.003 + $0.002 + $0.002 = $0.007 . Step 0: A small, dedicated wallet Create a new wallet just for the agent and put a few dollars of USDC on Base in it. You don't need ETH for gas; the facilitator pays it. Keep the private key in an environment variable: export WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY = 0x... # dedicated agent wallet, never your main one Then set up a project: mkdir x402-agent && cd x402-agent npm init -y && npm pkg set type = module npm i @x402/fetch @x402/evm viem openai npm i -D typescript tsx @types/node Node 20 or newer gives you a global fetch , which is all the payment wrapper needs. Run any file below with npx tsx file.ts . Step 1: Look at the 402 without paying An unpaid request is free. It returns 402 with the terms in the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header as base64 JSON: // peek-402.ts const res = await fetch ( "https://api.agentsearchhq.com/x402/v1/search" , { method : "POST" , headers : { "content-type" : "application/json" } , body : JSON . stringify ( { query : "x402 payment protocol" , max_results : 5 } ) , } ) ; console . log ( res . status ) ; // 402, nothing charged const header = res . headers . get ( "payment-required" ) ; if ( ! header ) throw new Error ( "no PAYMENT-REQUIRED header" ) ; const terms = JSON . parse ( Buffer . from ( header , "base64" ) . toString ( "utf8" ) ) ; const offer = terms . accepts [ 0 ] ; console . log ( offer . scheme , offer . network , offer . amount , offer . payTo ) ; // exact eip155:8453 3000 0xC49B157887e51c21CB655f39CF65D6a4c2a4C337 amount is in USDC atomic units (6 decimals), so 3000 is $0.003. This is also how an agent can discover a price at runtime: ask, read the 402, decide. Before you pay anything, check that payTo matches the address published at /.well-known/x402 and on the security page . Step 2: Pay per call with @x402/fetch @x402/fetch wraps the normal fetch . When a response is 402, it signs the payment with your wallet and retries the request: // search.ts import { wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig } from "@x402/fetch" ; import { ExactEvmScheme } from "@x402/evm" ; import { privateKeyToAccount } from "viem/accounts" ; const account = privateKeyToAccount ( process . env . WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY as `0x${string}` ) ; const payFetch = wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig ( fetch , { schemes : [ { network : "eip155:8453" , client : new ExactEvmScheme ( account ) } ] , } ) ; const res = await payFetch ( "https://api.agentsearchhq.com/x402/v1/search" , { method : "POST" , headers : { "content-type" : "application/json" } , body : JSON . stringify ( { query : "x402 payment protocol" , max_results : 5 } ) , } ) ; const data = await res . json ( ) ; for ( const hit of data . results ) console . log ( hit . score , hit . url ) ; A search response looks like this (trimmed): { "query" : "x402 payment protocol" , "result_count" : 5 , "results" : [ { "title" : "x402 - payments protocol for the internet" , "url" : "https://www.x402.org/" , "content" : "x402 is an open payment standard built on HTTP 402 ..." , "score" : 0.91 , "domain" : "x402.org" , "published_date" : null } ] } The receipt for each paid call comes back in the PAYMENT-RESPONSE header if you want to log it. Search, news and search-and-read also accept optional filters: freshness ( day , week , month , year ), country , language , and include_domains / exclude_domains . Step 3: Agent tools with a hard budget Agents call tools in loops. Don't leave spending to the prompt; put it in code. This module exposes webSearch and readPage , counts what was actually spent, and refuses any call that would cross the budget. Because failed and empty calls aren't settled, it only counts a call when it returns 200. // web-tools.ts import { wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig } from "@x402/fetch" ; import { ExactEvmScheme } from "@x402/evm" ; import { privateKeyToAccount } from "viem/accounts" ; const API = "https://api.agentsearchhq.com/x402/v1" ; const PRICE_USD = { search : 0.003 , extract : 0.002 } as const ; type Endpoint = keyof typeof PRICE_USD ; export class BudgetExceeded extends Error { } export class WebTools { spent = 0 ; private payFetch : typeof fetch ; constructor ( private budgetUsd = 0.1 ) { const account = privateKeyToAccount ( process . env . WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY as `0x${string}` ) ; this . payFetch = wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig ( fetch , { schemes : [ { network : "eip155:8453" , client : new ExactEvmScheme ( account ) } ] , } ) as typeof fetch ; } private async call ( endpoint : Endpoint , body : object ) : Promise < any > { const price = PRICE_USD [ endpoint ] ; if ( this . spent + price > this . budgetUsd ) { throw new BudgetExceeded ( `${endpoint} would exceed $${this.budgetUsd.toFixed(2)}` ) ; } const res = await this . payFetch ( `${API}/${endpoint}` , { method : "POST" , headers : { "content-type" : "application/json" } , body : JSON . stringify ( body ) , } ) ; if ( res . status !== 200 ) { // 400, 502 and empty answers are not settled, so nothing to count return { error : `HTTP ${res.status}` , detail : ( await res . text ( ) ) . slice ( 0 , 300 ) } ; } this . spent += price ; return res . json ( ) ; } async webSearch ( query : string , maxResults = 5 ) { const data = await this . call ( "search" , { query , max_results : maxResults } ) ; if ( data . error ) return data ; return { results : ( data . results ?? [ ] ) . map ( ( h : any ) => ( { title : h . title , url : h . url , snippet : String ( h . content ?? "" ) . slice ( 0 , 300 ) , } ) ) , } ; } async readPage ( url : string , maxChars = 8000 ) { const data = await this . call ( "extract" , { url , max_chars : maxChars } ) ; if ( data . error ) return data ; const md : string = data . markdown ?? "" ; return { url : data . url ?? url , title : data . title , markdown : md , empty : md . trim ( ) === "" } ; } } Two habits worth keeping even if you rewrite the rest: Trim what goes back to the model. 300-character snippets and 8,000-character pages keep the context window, and your model bill, under control. Extract takes max_chars (up to 50,000) so the trimming happens server side. Return errors as data. The model sees { error: "HTTP 400" } and can try another URL instead of crashing the run. Step 4: Wire the tools into an agent loop Here's a minimal tool-calling loop with the OpenAI Node SDK. Any model or framework with tool calls works the same way: describe the tools, run what the model asks for, feed the results back. // agent.ts import OpenAI from "openai" ; import { WebTools , BudgetExceeded } from "./web-tools.js" ; const tools : OpenAI . Chat . Completions . ChatCompletionTool [ ] = [ { type : "function" , function : { name : "web_search" , description : "Search the live web. Returns up to 5 results with title, url, snippet." , parameters : { type : "object" , properties : { query : { type : "string" } } , required : [ "query" ] , } , } , } , { type : "function" , function : { name : "read_page" , description : "Read one URL as clean markdown. Use on the 1-2 best search results." , parameters : { type : "object" , properties : { url : { type : "string" } } , required : [ "url" ] , } , } , } , ] ; const SYSTEM = "Answer with sources. Search once, read at most two pages, then answer and cite the URLs you read." ; async function run ( question : string ) { const llm = new OpenAI ( ) ; const web = new WebTools ( 0.05 ) ; // five cents max per question const messages : OpenAI . Chat . Completions . ChatCompletionMessageParam [ ] = [ { role : "system" , content : SYSTEM } , { role : "user" , content : question } , ] ; try { for ( let round = 0 ; round < 6 ; round ++ ) { // hard cap on tool rounds const resp = await llm . chat . completions . create ( { model : "gpt-4o-mini" , messages , tools } ) ; const msg = resp . choices [ 0 ] . message ; messages . push ( msg ) ; if ( ! msg . tool_calls ? . length ) { console . log ( msg . content ) ; break ; } for ( const call of msg . tool_calls ) { if ( call . type !== "function" ) continue ; const args = JSON . parse ( call . function . arguments ) ; let result : unknown ; try { result = call . function . name === "web_search" ? await web . webSearch ( args . query ) : await web . readPage ( args . url ) ; } catch ( e ) { result = e instanceof BudgetExceeded ? { error : e . message , hint : "Answer with what you have." } : { error : String ( e ) } ; } messages . push ( { role : "tool" , tool_call_id : call . id , content : JSON . stringify ( result ) } ) ; } } } finally { console . log ( `spent $${web.spent.toFixed(3)}` ) ; } } await run ( "What changed in the x402 v2 spec?" ) ; A typical run is one search and two page reads, $0.007 . With a $0.05 budget the worst case per question is five cents, and the six-round cap stops a runaway loop long before that. When Extract comes back empty Some pages are single-page apps that ship an empty HTML shell and draw everything with JavaScript. Extract returns little or no markdown for those, and since empty extractions aren't settled, the miss costs nothing. For those URLs, call POST /x402/v1/render with the same { url } body. It loads the page in headless Chromium and returns markdown with the title and links. Add it as a third tool, or fall back to it inside readPage when empty is true. Current Render pricing is on the Render page , and reading JavaScript pages from an AI agent walks through when you need it. One call instead of four: Search + Read If your agent nearly always reads the top results anyway, search_and_read returns the top 1 to 5 results with each page's markdown in a single paid call, $0.005 , settled only when at least one page has text: const res = await payFetch ( "https://api.agentsearchhq.com/x402/v1/search_and_read" , { method : "POST" , headers : { "content-type" : "application/json" } , body : JSON . stringify ( { query : "x402 v2 spec changes" , num_results : 3 } ) , } ) ; const { results } = await res . json ( ) ; for ( const page of results ) console . log ( page . url , page . chars , page . extract_status ) ; That's one payment instead of four for a search plus three reads ($0.005 versus $0.009 a la carte). Details on Search + Read . Prefer not to write payment code? You don't have to. The AgentSearch packages pay the direct x402 API for you once you set AGENTSEARCH_WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY , and they include a free search tier : up to 25 searches a day per IP, up to 5 results each, no key and no wallet. That's a good way to build and test at $0 before you fund anything. Search stays on the free tier until you opt in to paid search ( mode: "paid" in the AI SDK package, AGENTSEARCH_MODE=paid in MCP); a wallet key on its own only pays for the other tools. Vercel AI SDK: npm i @agentsearchhq/ai-sdk ai zod gives you ready-made AI SDK tools ( agentSearchFreeTools() for the free set, agentSearchTools() for all six): free web search, free-trial extract and render, and pay-per-call news, screenshots and search-and-read. Guide: add web search to the Vercel AI SDK . LangChain.js: see add web search to a LangChain.js agent . MCP (Claude, Cursor, Cline, VS Code): npx -y @agentsearchhq/agentsearch-mcp , with AGENTSEARCH_WALLET_PRIVATE_KEY in the server's env for paid calls. With nothing set, Extract and Render run on a free trial of 5 and 3 calls a day per IP. Setup: free MCP web scraping . n8n: the n8n-nodes-agentsearch community node. See n8n AI agent: read web pages . Wallet checklist Use a new wallet that holds only what the agent may spend. Keep the key in an environment variable or a secret manager, never in a repo or a prompt. Cap spend in code (budget per task) and cap tool rounds per run. Check payTo , amount, token and network against the 402 terms and /.well-known/x402 . Never sign a Permit, Permit2 or approve request to pay for a call. An x402 exact payment is a single transfer of the listed amount with a short validity window. FAQ Do I need an AgentSearch account or API key? No. The 402 response is the price list, and the signed payment is the authorization. Which network and token? USDC on Base mainnet ( eip155:8453 ), x402 v2 exact scheme, through the Coinbase CDP facilitator. No ETH needed for gas. Does this work in the browser or on edge runtimes? The @x402/fetch wrapper only needs a fetch implementation and a signer, so it runs anywhere fetch does. Don't ship a private key to a browser, though. For agents, keep the wallet on a server, a worker or a CLI process you control. Can I use axios instead of fetch? Yes. @x402/axios exposes wrapAxiosWithPaymentFromConfig with the same schemes config. There's a copy-paste example in the direct x402 API docs . What happens if a call fails? Nothing is settled. Payment is verified first and only settled after a successful, non-empty answer. A reused payment gets HTTP 409. Is there a Python version? Yes: x402 Python tutorial . Get started Run peek-402.ts from Step 1 to see the live terms for free. Fund a small agent wallet with a few dollars of USDC on Base. Drop WebTools into your agent and set a budget. Full endpoint reference: docs/x402 . Machine-readable: OpenAPI .

title: OpenAI fornece modelos de IA à Otan para proteger redes contra ameaças
author: guiadeti
summary: Modelos de IA apoiarão a cibersegurança da Otan A OpenAI disponibilizou seus modelos de inteligência artificial para ajudar a Otan a proteger suas redes contra ameaças cibernéticas. A tecnologia será usada para investigar atividades suspeitas, identificar vulnerabilidades e acelerar a aplicação de correções em sistemas da aliança. A iniciativa envolve a Agência de Comunicações e Informação da Otan (NCIA), centro tecnológico e de segurança digital que reúne mais de 3 mil especialistas civis e militares. O trabalho ocorre pelo programa Daybreak, voltado a atividades autorizadas de cibersegurança. Agência já chegou a usar 300 bilhões de tokens A OpenAI anunciou a parceria no primeiro dia da conferência NATO Edge 26, realizada na Turquia. Segundo a empresa, a Otan já chegou a utilizar até 300 bilhões de tokens por mês em atividades de segurança cibernética. Tokens são unidades de informação que sistemas de inteligência artificial processam para interpretar solicitações e gerar respostas. Nesse caso, o volume informado pela OpenAI dimensiona o uso dos modelos nas tarefas de proteção digital da aliança. Para Dylan Browne, gerente-geral da NCIA, os modelos podem acelerar a descoberta de vulnerabilidades, ajudar a identificar ameaças emergentes e facilitar a adoção de contramedidas. Ele afirmou ao The Wall Street Journal que as ferramentas podem fortalecer a resiliência cibernética e a proteção de infraestruturas digitais críticas. Daybreak reúne iniciativas com órgãos públicos O Daybreak permite que órgãos públicos e clientes corporativos acessem modelos da OpenAI para trabalhos autorizados de segurança cibernética. Entre as aplicações previstas estão localizar falhas em sistemas e desenvolver medidas para corrigi-las com mais rapidez. Em setembro, a OpenAI anunciou que o Ministério da Transformação Digital da Ucrânia usaria o programa para proteger infraestruturas civis. O trabalho inclui ferramentas para localizar vulnerabilidades em softwares e desenvolver e testar correções. A Agência da União Europeia para a Cibersegurança (ENISA) também recorreu a modelos da OpenAI para identificar vulnerabilidades em programas usados por instituições da União Europeia. A parceria com a Otan amplia a presença dessas ferramentas em iniciativas de proteção digital de órgãos públicos europeus. Parceria ocorre em meio a ameaças na Europa O anúncio foi feito em um período de tensões geopolíticas elevadas e de episódios recentes que afetaram diferentes setores europeus. Entre eles, um ataque a sistemas de refrigeração de supermercados causou perdas de alimentos e falhas em equipamentos. Também foram relatadas falsas ameaças de bomba enviadas por e-mail a aeroportos, companhias aéreas e centenas de escolas. As mensagens levaram ao desvio de voos e a pousos de emergência, enquanto a análise rápida de informações é apontada pela NCIA como um recurso para apoiar respostas a ameaças digitais. Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/openai-ajuda-otan-a-proteger-redes-contra-ameacas-ciberneticas/
